description: Sync issues, comments and worklogs from the Jira Cloud projects you choose. Project and issue-security restrictions apply only with Enforce ACL on and a successful permission read.
opening: Sync issues, comments and worklogs from the Jira Cloud projects you select. Each issue is one document with its description, environment, people, status, labels, issue links and linked pull requests. Each comment and each worklog entry is its own document, linked to its issue.

Project and issue-security permissions restrict search only when Enforce ACL is on and HydraDB can read them, which needs a Jira site-admin account. Issue history, watchers and most custom fields are not synced. Edits come across on the next sync. Items deleted in Jira stay in HydraDB.

permissions.who_can_read: Access follows the project. An issue can be read by the active people who hold Browse Projects on its project. An issue with a security level can be read only by that level's members, and an empty level lets nobody read it. A comment or worklog follows its issue's security level.
permissions.identity: A person's email address. For a security level, Jira groups are kept as groups next to their members' emails.
permissions.when_unreadable: If HydraDB cannot read a project's Browse holders or an issue's security level, the connector reports a permission warning.
notes: Reading who can browse a project needs a Jira site-admin account.
One Browse holder whose email is hidden by Atlassian profile visibility stops HydraDB from capturing the whole project's audience. Set an access rule on such a project.
A project with too many readers to express cannot be captured.
A security level held by project roles, the reporter, the assignee or a custom field cannot be captured.
A comment or worklog whose issue security level cannot be found follows the project's access.
If Jira returns a temporary error, the audience captured earlier stays in force.

connect.auth: Jira uses an Atlassian API token together with the email of the account that owns it.

credentials.name: domain
credentials.text: Your Atlassian site host, for example `acme.atlassian.net`.

credentials.name: email
credentials.text: The email of the Atlassian account that owns the API token.

credentials.name: api_token
credentials.text: An Atlassian API token for that account.

permissions.name: Browse projects
permissions.text: required. Lists projects and their issues.

permissions.name: Browse issues
permissions.text: required. Reads issue fields, comments and worklogs.

permissions.name: Administer Jira
permissions.text: optional, for permissions. Reading who can browse a project and issue security schemes needs a site-admin account.

permissions.name: Browse users and groups
permissions.text: optional, for permissions. Finds each project reader's email and turns a security level's groups into member emails.

steps.title: Create an API token
steps.text: In your Atlassian account security settings, create an API token for the account HydraDB will use. Give that account the Jira permissions above on every project you will select.

steps.title: Create the connector
steps.text: Enter your site as `domain`, the account's `email`, and the token as `api_token`.

steps.title: Select projects
steps.text: HydraDB lists every project the account can see, with its name and key. Select the projects to sync.

connect.account: One connector reads one Jira Cloud site as the account that owns the token, and sees only what that account can access.

sync.first_sync: A newly selected project reads back the window set by `lookback_days`, 30 days by default. The window is measured on when an issue was last updated, not when it was created.
sync.changes: Each sync reads the issues updated since the last sync. Comments and worklogs are read again for every issue in that window.
sync.edits: An edited issue is picked up through its last-updated time and updates its document. Comments and worklogs are read again whenever their issue is picked up.
sync.deletes: Issues, comments and worklogs deleted in Jira stay searchable in HydraDB.

shared_attributes.name: additional_metadata.project_key
shared_attributes.text: The project key. Limits a query to one project. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: additional_metadata.project_name
shared_attributes.text: The project name. Another way to limit a query to one project. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: additional_metadata.container_id
shared_attributes.text: The project key, the same value as `additional_metadata.project_key`. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: additional_metadata.container_name
shared_attributes.text: The project name, the same value as `additional_metadata.project_name`. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: additional_metadata.security_level_id
shared_attributes.text: The issue's security level, when one is set. A comment or worklog carries its issue's level. Limits a query to one level, and the level's members decide who can read the item. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: additional_metadata.security_level_name
shared_attributes.text: The name of the issue's security level, when one is set. Limits a query by level name. The level itself, not this name, decides who can read the item. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: connector_id
shared_attributes.text: Limits a query to this connector's items. Not searchable.

shared_attributes.name: Project
shared_attributes.text: The selected project. The people who can browse it decide who can read its items, unless an issue has a security level. Not searchable.

documents.name: Issues
documents.one_document: One Jira issue. Its comments and worklogs are separate documents.
documents.title: The issue summary, or `Jira issue` and the issue key, or the numeric id, when there is no summary.
documents.text: A first line with the issue key and type, such as `ENG-123 (Bug)`. Then a `Parent` line and one line per issue link, such as `blocks: ENG-7`, up to 20. Then the description as plain text, with link targets kept and mentions written as names, the `Environment` text, and a `Linked pull requests` list with one pull request address per line. The status, priority, assignee, reporter, type, labels, creation date and resolution date are written as lines too. The title is searchable too.
documents.date: When the issue was last updated, or when it was created if there is no update time.
documents.files: Files attached to the issue are downloaded with the connector's credentials and read, and their text becomes searchable with the issue. A file with no id or download address is skipped. A file that fails to download or is not a supported type keeps only its details.

attributes.name: Issue key
attributes.text: The issue key, such as `ENG-123`, or the numeric issue id when there is no key. It keeps later syncs on the same document.

attributes.name: status
attributes.text: The workflow status name, written as the `Status` line.

attributes.name: priority
attributes.text: The priority name, written as the `Priority` line.

attributes.name: issue_type
attributes.text: The issue type name, written as the `Type` line and in the first line of the text.

attributes.name: labels
attributes.text: The issue's labels, written as the `Labels` line.

attributes.name: assignee
attributes.text: The assignee's display name, written as the `Assignee` line. The graph records that person as the assignee.

attributes.name: reporter
attributes.text: The reporter's display name, or the creator's when there is no reporter, written as the `Reporter` line. The graph records that person as the reporter.

attributes.name: Attached files
attributes.text: The text read from each attached file, searchable with the issue.

attributes.name: Linked pull requests
attributes.text: The addresses of pull requests linked in the issue's Development panel, one per line in the text. If Atlassian changes how it reports them, issues show no linked pull requests rather than an error. They are not linked to GitHub or GitLab items in the graph.

attributes.name: created_at
attributes.text: When the issue was created, written into the issue details. Sets the result date only when the update time is missing.

attributes.name: resolved_at
attributes.text: When the issue was resolved, written into the issue details.

attributes.name: updated_at
attributes.text: When the issue was last updated. Sets the result date and decides when a sync picks the issue up. Not searchable.

attributes.name: parent_id
attributes.text: The key of the parent issue or epic, written as the `Parent` line. Links the issue to its parent.

attributes.name: linked_issue_ids
attributes.text: The keys of every linked issue. Up to 20 different keys are written into the text. Every linked issue is linked in the graph.

attributes.name: mentions
attributes.text: Names of people @mentioned in the description. The graph records each as mentioned by the issue. The field itself is not searchable, but the description it comes from is.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_key
attributes.text: The issue key, such as `ENG-123`. Picks out one issue. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_id
attributes.text: The numeric issue id. Picks out one issue by id. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_parent_id
attributes.text: The numeric id of the parent issue or epic. Returns the children of one parent. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_link_types
attributes.text: The link phrases on this issue's side, such as `blocks` or `is blocked by`. Finds issues with a given kind of link. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_self
attributes.text: The issue's address in the Jira REST API. Mainly shows where the item came from. Not searchable.

attributes.name: due_date
attributes.text: The issue due date. It is not written into the text.

attributes.name: custom_fields
attributes.text: The resolution name, component names, fix version names and linked pull request addresses. Only the pull request addresses also appear in the text.

documents.name: Comments
documents.title: `Comment on ENG-123`, or `Comment on issue` and the numeric issue id when the key is unknown.
documents.text: The comment as plain text. The author, the creation and update times, and the issue key are written with it.
documents.date: When the comment was last updated, or when it was created if there is no update time.
documents.link_back: The issue's page in Jira with the comment focused.

attributes.name: author
attributes.text: The commenter's display name. The graph records the comment as written by that person.

attributes.name: author_email
attributes.text: The commenter's email, when Jira shows it. Identifies the commenter in the graph. Not searchable.

attributes.name: created_at
attributes.text: When the comment was created. Sets the result date only when the update time is missing.

attributes.name: updated_at
attributes.text: When the comment was last updated. Sets the result date.

attributes.name: parent_id
attributes.text: The key of the issue the comment is on. Links the comment to that issue.

attributes.name: thread_id
attributes.text: The issue key. Groups the comments and worklogs of one issue together in the graph. Not searchable.

attributes.name: mentions
attributes.text: Names of people @mentioned in the comment. The graph records each as mentioned. The field itself is not searchable, but the comment text is.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_comment_id
attributes.text: The numeric comment id. Picks out one comment. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_issue_key
attributes.text: The key of the issue. Returns every comment on one issue. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_issue_id
attributes.text: The numeric id of the issue. Returns every comment on one issue. Not searchable.

documents.name: Worklogs
documents.one_document: One worklog entry on an issue.
documents.title: `Worklog on ENG-123`, or `Worklog on issue` and the numeric issue id when the key is unknown.
documents.text: A first line such as `Sam logged work on ENG-123 (1h 30m)`, then the worklog note as plain text. The author, the update time and the issue key are written with it.
documents.date: When the worklog was last updated, or when the logged work started if there is no update time.
documents.link_back: The issue's page in Jira with the worklog focused.

attributes.name: author
attributes.text: The name of the person who logged the work. The graph records the worklog as written by that person.

attributes.name: author_email
attributes.text: The email of the person who logged the work, when Jira shows it. Identifies that person in the graph. Not searchable.

attributes.name: updated_at
attributes.text: When the worklog was last updated, written as the `Updated` line. Sets the result date.

attributes.name: started_at
attributes.text: When the logged work started. Sets the result date only when there is no update time. Not searchable.

attributes.name: parent_id
attributes.text: The key of the issue the work was logged on. Links the worklog to that issue.

attributes.name: thread_id
attributes.text: The issue key. Groups the comments and worklogs of one issue together in the graph. Not searchable.

attributes.name: mentions
attributes.text: Names of people @mentioned in the worklog note. The graph records each as mentioned. The field itself is not searchable, but the note is.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_worklog_id
attributes.text: The numeric worklog id. Picks out one worklog. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_issue_key
attributes.text: The key of the issue. Returns every worklog on one issue. Not searchable.

attributes.name: additional_metadata.jira_issue_id
attributes.text: The numeric id of the issue. Returns every worklog on one issue. Not searchable.

attributes.name: time_spent_seconds
attributes.text: The exact number of seconds logged. The text carries a readable duration instead.

example_searches: Which bugs in the ENG project are still In Progress and assigned to Sam?
How much time was logged on ENG-789, and by whom?

connections: An issue to its parent issue or epic.

An issue to each issue it links to. `blocks`, `is blocked by` and `is caused by` keep their direction. `relates to`, `duplicates`, `clones` and `causes` become a plain related link. Other link types become a general link.
A comment or worklog to its issue, and the comments and worklogs of one issue to each other.
No links to items in other tools. Linked pull requests stay addresses in the text.
people: The assignee and the reporter, or creator, of each issue.
The author of each comment and worklog.
People @mentioned in a description, comment or worklog note.
graph.from_text: The issue description and environment, and the text of each comment and worklog note.

not_synced: Projects, boards, sprints, versions, components and users as items of their own.
Jira admin configuration: screens, schemes, filters, dashboards and custom field definitions.
Custom fields other than resolution, components and fix versions.
Linked pull requests, when development-status capture is turned off with `include_dev_status`.
Comments with no text, and comments or worklogs whose issue cannot be identified.
